I think you misunderstand what being transgender means. "Allowing" it is meaningless because nobody chooses to be transgender, in the same way they don't choose to be gay, or straight, or what have you. 

Transgender is not simply "I was born male/female and want to be a female/male," or "I was born male/female and always wondered what it felt like to be another gender." It might appear that way, and some people might play it up that way for the camera, but it's not really a 'choice' or a 'want.' Transgender is "I am a male/female that was born in a female/male body and it is so excruciatingly uncomfortable, dysphoric, and in some cases *painful* to exist the way I do that I am willing to undergo hormone therapy and surgery in order to get some semblance of what it means to be in a body that feels like it's mine." The people who aren't really sure, the ones that you're talking about, they'll experiment with partners, they'll crossdress, they may even try to pass, but they don't undergo treatments and surgery on a "maybe." Transgender people are desperately trying to be comfortable with themselves and their bodies because to keep going on as they are is tantamount to a slow, painful, miserable death.

And yeah, there will be plenty of kids who think "maybe" they wish they were different; I can't remember a time in my childhood that I was really satisfied with who I was, even though it didn't have much, if anything, to do with gender: part of growing up is feeling out who you really want to be, and learning to either change the things you don't like about yourself or accepting them, and yourself. But how many times did your parents tell you "It's just a phase, you'll grow out of it" only to be decidedly wrong about you when you grew into adulthood? Because if the answer is higher than "never," then you know why it's important that kids be allowed to make those decisions about themselves. 

And, granted, there will be kids with bad judgement: hell, there are plenty of adults with bad judgement too. But I think it's better for them to be able to make the decision and know for themselves whether they were right or wrong than to deny them the opportunity and make them feel like they never got a chance at being a whole person. The issue is, as you may already know, hormone treatments tend not to be nearly as effective after puberty, and after that window has passed, you have a lot less opportunity to make the transition well enough to find peace and comfort. I do think it's important, though, that kids who are seriously considering it understand, and be stressed upon the permanence of those changes, that it's more akin to getting a limb removed than to getting a tattoo (even though I think that might be a bit graphic,) and that they should only go through with it if they're prepared to live with the consequences.
